evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: How did you get into this?

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: So originally you built the site to allow people to create their own custom jewelry? Is that what I'm hearing? And then you moved into supporting other jewelers?

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: You said it takes one to two months to integrate. What is involved in that?

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: I fully believe that. I have multiple friends who run online jewelry brands that do super well for them, as small businesses. So I believe that the sales cycle's super quick. Actually, this is probably one of the few businesses where I'm not worried about the sales cycle. But the thing I think I'm still hung up about is this integration. Even at scale, three weeks to get a partner onboarded still feels really long to me, and you'll need a big team to start all of a sudden onboarding all these different folks, right. The capital structure on this feels very heavy. Talk about that.

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: So actually if we could just talk about pricing more wholistically and kind of break it down.

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: It sounds like you've got a roughly 1k per month monthly fee, and that has super high margins.

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: And then you have this try-on product, which presumably has near zero margins.

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: Got it. And then you charge 3 to 10% on transaction fees.

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: How much money have you raised before on this company?

evidence_registry.speaker: Elizabeth
evidence_registry.text: So I think you are very impressive. I think you're on to an interesting problem and I completely agree with you on the sales cycle. I think it's gonna be a really good sales cycle for you. I think, you know, given where the business is, like after this round you'll have raised $7 million and you'll - it seems like you're just sort of at the beginning of the customer acquisition cycle, I'm worried about the capitalization and the cap table. I'm also worried about the valuation, given where the company is as well. And so for that reason, I'm out.

Elizabeth was concerned that onboarding partners would take too long and require a large team as the company scaled.

Elizabeth requested a holistic breakdown of pricing and confirmed the transaction-fee component.

Elizabeth expressed the view that the try-on product presumably had near-zero margins.
Elizabeth agreed with the founder's claim about poor jewelry conversion and bounce rates, supporting the existence of a meaningful problem.
Elizabeth asked about the company's prior fundraising and confirmed that $4 million had already been raised, probing capitalization and dilution context.

Elizabeth noted that, despite the capital raised after the round, the company appeared to be only at the beginning of its customer acquisition cycle.

Elizabeth explicitly said she was worried about the valuation given where the company was and cited this as part of the reason for going out.

annotation_summary: Elizabeth positively assessed the problem, founder, and sales cycle, but raised concerns about integration scalability and capital intensity during diligence. Her explicit reasons for going Out were capitalization/cap-table concerns and valuation relative to company stage.
